doc.title: Artie Shaw — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: How playbacks worked without acetates; the Interlude recording
summary: Shaw cannot recall how playback worked before acetate or tape, and speculates about how the Interlude in B-flat second version got recorded.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: A real basic technical question, because we weren’t around then: when they recorded on . . . when they cut the wax, did they also run an acetate for you to listen to as a playback?
They didn’t have acetate at first.
What did they play back? What did they actually play back to you?
I really don’t know. Might have been . . .

Maybe there was some other thing that they had, or maybe a double . . . Yes, I think they had two turntables. One that you’d hear back, of the one you had just made. I’m pretty sure it was something like that. They put it on something, whatever it was. They didn’t have acetate. Whatever they had. It’s hard to remember, because they didn’t have tape. I remember, for example, we talked earlier about Interlude in B-flat. They didn’t even have . . . they had wire recorders at that time, and they weren’t very good. Somebody must have put that thing . . . see, it was on a microphone in the theater. Somebody must have taken it off the air, because I don’t know how that second version . . . the one that came out, there was no applause. The one that we did first, every time there’s a change of tempo, the audience would scream. So, when they said, “Play it again,” second time we played it, that was recorded. Somebody must have thought, “Hey, this is a good piece. We better get it on.”
Yeah, they might have had a wire down to a local recording studio.
Who knows? I have no idea.
